knowledge_type_note: A specific named position with a proven result; the defender's counterpart to the Lucena.

attributions.note: Analysed the position in 1777. The attribution here is secure, unlike the Lucena's.
Showed that Philidor's claim of uniqueness was not strictly correct; Johann Berger expanded on it.

history.notes: Better founded than the Lucena's naming. Recorded medium rather than high only because Philidor's own text was not consulted here.

development.change: The third-rank defence is analysed and presented as the drawing method.
Philidor's claim that it was the only drawing method is shown to be too strong.

engine_era_note: Tablebase-confirmed. Engines also make clear how narrow the alternatives are, which is why the third-rank defence remains the practical method.

preconditions: Rook and pawn against rook, defending side to hold
Defending king in front of the pawn
Pawn not yet on the defender's third rank
Defending rook on the defender's third rank
indicators_for: The attacking king cannot reach its sixth rank because the rook denies it
The defender's rook has the seventh and eighth ranks available for rear checks
indicators_against: The defending king is cut off from the pawn's file — likely a Lucena instead
The pawn has already reached the third rank while the rook is still on it
The defending rook has no safe far rank to drop to
false_positive_traps: The rook must leave the third rank at exactly the right moment — too early and the king comes in, too late and the pawn is past. Recognising the setup is not the same as executing it.
If the defending king is not in front of the pawn, this is not a Philidor and the position may be lost.

typical_plans: Hold the third rank; when the pawn advances to it, go to the far rank and check from behind
Accept a rook trade if offered on the third rank — the pawn ending is drawn
typical_moves: A waiting rook move along the third rank
Rook to the eighth rank once the pawn advances
strategic_consequences: The defensive target in most rook endings a pawn down

exceptions: Philidor's own claim of uniqueness is too strong: other defences draw, though they are harder.
With the pawn less advanced, the defending rook uses its FOURTH rank instead of the third and the king needs only to reach its second.
misconceptions: That it is the only way to draw — Karstedt showed otherwise in 1897.
That passive defence works. It does not; the rook must switch to rear checks at the right moment.

examples.note: Philidor setup with colours reversed from the usual diagram: White is the DEFENDER, king on e1 in front of the pawn, rook on a3 holding the third rank. Black has king e5, pawn e4, rook b2.

tablebase.note: PROVEN draw. The tablebase's best move is a waiting rook move along the rank, which is exactly the third-rank defence's first phase — hold the rank and do nothing until the pawn commits.

engine.verdict_note: PROVEN DRAW, dtz 0, best move Ra1, engine 0.00 at depth 26. The Philidor defence holds, and it holds over every legal continuation rather than over the twenty the engine looked at. Note what this base has NOT been able to build: a verified counterexample. With the pawn on the fourth rank the defence draws from almost anywhere, so the position that would show the method failing has resisted three attempts and the record says so.

by_level.beginner: Keep your king in front of their pawn and your rook across the third row so their king cannot come forward. When the pawn finally advances, drop your rook far back and check them from behind.
by_level.intermediate: The Philidor position — a draw. Two phases: hold the third rank, then check from behind once the pawn arrives on it. Getting the switch wrong is how the draw is lost.
by_level.advanced: Third-rank defence. Both attacking tries fail: pushing the pawn removes the king's screen, and interposing on the third rank allows a rook trade into a drawn pawn ending.
by_level.master: The defensive target in rook endings a pawn down. Note Philidor's uniqueness claim was disproved by Karstedt in 1897, though the alternatives are harder.

by_depth.short: King in front, rook on the third rank, then check from behind.
by_depth.normal: The Philidor position: the drawing method in rook and pawn against rook. Hold your rook on the third rank so their king cannot advance; when the pawn is pushed to that rank, swing the rook to the far end and check from behind.
by_depth.deep: The defender's counterpart to the Lucena, analysed by Philidor in 1777. Conditions: defending king in front of the pawn, pawn not yet on the defender's third rank, attacking king beyond it, defending rook on it. The method has two phases and the timing is everything — hold the rank until the pawn commits, then check from behind, where the attacking king has lost the screen its own pawn provided. Both attacking tries fail cleanly: pushing removes the cover, interposing allows a rook trade into a drawn pawn ending. Philidor believed it was the only drawing method; Karstedt showed in 1897 that it is not, though the alternatives are more complicated.

explanations.lesson: A pawn down in a rook ending, get your king in front of the pawn and your rook on the third rank. Then wait — and only switch to checking from behind when the pawn actually advances.

beginner_words: king in front of the pawn

definition_short: The drawing setup in rook and pawn against rook: defending king in front of the pawn, defending rook on the third rank, then checking from behind once the pawn advances.
